definition: Impossible to explain satisfactorily.
example: The sudden reversal was inexplicable without new evidence.
cloze: An _____ reversal demands an explanation.
note: Latin explicare means to unfold or explain; explic- is a bound stem, not an English word.

definition: Fluent, expressive, and persuasive in speech.
example: Her eloquent closing made a complex idea accessible.
cloze: An _____ speaker makes complex ideas accessible.
note: The Latin stem loqu- changes to loqu- plus -ent in this teaching analysis.

definition: Well meaning and inclined to do good.
example: Even a benevolent policy needs independent scrutiny.
cloze: A _____ leader acts with goodwill.
note: From Latin bene (well) and volens (wishing).

definition: Wishing harm to others.
example: Do not presume malevolent intent when evidence is incomplete.
cloze: Wishing harm reflects _____ intent.
note: Male- comes from Latin male, badly, rather than the English word male.

definition: A direct conflict between statements or ideas.
example: There is a contradiction between the promise and the budget.
cloze: Two mutually incompatible claims form a _____.
note: A learning decomposition of the Latin-derived stem contradict- and -ion.

definition: A statement about what will happen.
example: Make a prediction that the next trial can test.
cloze: A testable statement about the future is a _____.
note: Latin praedicere combines prae, before, with dicere, say.

definition: Worthy of belief or trust.
example: A credible source explains how its data were collected.
cloze: A trustworthy account is _____.
note: Cred- is a bound Latin-derived root.

definition: Difficult to believe; also used to mean extraordinary.
example: The incredible claim requires unusually strong evidence.
cloze: A claim that is difficult to believe is _____.
note: Use the literal sense carefully: everyday speech also uses incredible as praise.

definition: Too ready to believe something.
example: A credulous audience may mistake confidence for proof.
cloze: An overly trusting listener is _____.
note: The adjective-forming ending continues Latin -ulus; the teaching split is simplified.

definition: Unwilling or unable to believe something.
example: The panel was incredulous at the unsupported claim.
cloze: An unconvinced, disbelieving audience is _____.
note: Incredulous describes the person who doubts; incredible describes what is hard to believe.

definition: Looking back at past events.
example: A retrospective review revealed the missing assumption.
cloze: A review looking back is _____.
note: The root spect- comes from Latin specere, to look.

definition: Examination of one’s own thoughts and feelings.
example: Introspection helped her separate evidence from pride.
cloze: Looking inward at your own thoughts is _____.
note: A transparent learning split of intro-, spect-, and -ion.

definition: Careful consideration before acting.
example: Circumspection is useful when a question hides an assumption.
cloze: Cautious consideration before acting is _____.
note: The image is looking around before proceeding.

definition: Able to be defended or maintained.
example: The position is tenable only if the cost estimate is sound.
cloze: A position that can be defended is _____.
note: From French tenable, ultimately Latin tenere, to hold.

definition: Unable to be defended or maintained.
example: The conclusion became untenable after the evidence changed.
cloze: An indefensible position is _____.
note: English un- attaches to tenable; the deeper stem is Latin-derived.

definition: Not able to be changed.
example: Treat the deadline as fixed, not the plan as immutable.
cloze: Something incapable of change is _____.
note: Im- is a form of negative in- before certain consonants.

definition: Capable of being changed.
example: Preferences are mutable when incentives change.
cloze: Something that can change is _____.
note: Latin mutare means to change.

definition: Effective at causing someone to accept an idea.
example: A persuasive argument connects evidence to the audience’s concern.
cloze: An argument that convinces is _____.
note: Suas- is a stem variant of Latin suadere, to urge.

definition: The act of persuading someone not to do something.
example: Dissuasion worked better when an alternative was offered.
cloze: Persuading someone not to act is _____.
note: Related to dissuade; the stem uses suas- before -ion.

definition: The undermining of an established system.
example: Criticism of a policy is not necessarily subversion of an institution.
cloze: Undermining an established order is _____.
note: The historical image is turning from beneath.

definition: A turning away from a main course or topic.
example: The personal accusation was a diversion from the evidence.
cloze: A distraction from the main issue is a _____.
note: Di- is a variant of dis- in the Latin-derived word.

definition: Able to be carried or moved easily.
example: A portable framework works in meetings as well as debates.
cloze: A framework that is easy to carry between contexts is _____.
note: From Latin portare, to carry.

definition: Relating to the voice; openly expressing views.
example: Vocal emphasis should make the central claim easy to hear.
cloze: Emphasis made with the voice is _____ emphasis.
note: From Latin vox, with stem voc-, voice.

definition: An appeal to an authority, principle, or power.
example: An invocation of tradition does not settle the evidence.
cloze: Calling upon a principle or authority is an _____.
note: Here in- is not the negative prefix; it belongs to Latin invocare.

definition: The arrangement of events in time order.
example: Establish the chronology before arguing about causation.
cloze: An ordered timeline is a _____.
note: -ology combines the connecting vowel o with -logy; the split is pedagogical.

definition: Relating to speech sounds.
example: A phonetic cue can make a new word easier to say.
cloze: A cue about speech sounds is _____.
note: A simplified decomposition of Greek-derived phonetic.

definition: Lacking a clearly defined form or structure.
example: The amorphous proposal needs a measurable objective.
cloze: A proposal with no clear shape is _____.
note: Greek a- is a negative prefix.

definition: The capacity to understand another person’s feelings.
example: Empathy helps you restate an objection fairly.
cloze: Understanding another person’s feelings shows _____.
note: A teaching split of a word based on Greek empatheia; em- is a form of en-.

definition: Words written or engraved on a surface.
example: The inscription gave the monument a voice across centuries.
cloze: Writing engraved on a monument is an _____.
note: Script- is a stem variant related to scribere, to write.

definition: An expression of blessing or good wishes.
example: The closing felt like a benediction rather than a demand.
cloze: An expression of blessing is a _____.
note: The literal roots suggest speaking well of someone.

definition: A failure to work correctly.
example: One malfunction does not prove the entire design is defective.
cloze: A failure of normal operation is a _____.
note: Mal- attaches to the English base function; there is no separate suffix here.

definition: To carry something from one place to another.
example: A concrete example can transport the audience into the situation.
cloze: To carry across locations is to _____.
note: No additional suffix is present in this form.
